messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame Adjei, a 19-year-old UX designer, first sought help after nearly a year of feeling an unrelenting sense of unease. A bright and creative individual, Kwame’s world had been irrevocably altered by a period of intense stalking that began subtly online before escalating into a chilling physical presence. Initially, it was just strange comments on his public design portfolios and social media, then messages referencing obscure details of his daily life, things he was certain he hadn't shared. A cold dread settled in when he started seeing the same unfamiliar person near his apartment building, then outside the co-working space where he interned. The feeling of being constantly watched, of his personal space and digital footprint being invaded, was terrifying and left him feeling utterly exposed.

In the aftermath of the stalking, Kwame found himself consumed by a pervasive sense of self-blame. He meticulously replayed every online interaction, every photo he’d posted, every location tag, convinced that he had somehow brought this upon himself. *If only I hadn’t shared so much, if only I had been more careful about my privacy settings,* he would ruminate, certain that the event happened because of the way he acted, that his openness had been an invitation for intrusion. This internal criticism became a constant companion, eroding his confidence and fostering a deep sense of regret.

This harrowing experience fundamentally reshaped Kwame's perception of the world around him. He had come to believe, with an unshakable conviction, that the world was a dangerous place. The previous sense of safety he’d taken for granted had evaporated, replaced by a pervasive feeling that threat lurked just beneath the surface of everyday life. Every stranger on the street, every unexpected noise, every unfamiliar car parked near his building became a potential harbinger of danger.

Consequently, Kwame developed an intense and exhausting need for constant vigilance. His mind was perpetually on high alert, always scanning his surroundings, assessing potential threats. He was certain that he had to be especially careful because you never knew what can happen next. This meant meticulously checking the locks on his apartment door multiple times before leaving, and again upon returning. At his UX design internship, his focus was often fractured; while attempting to concentrate on wireframes and user flows, his attention would involuntarily drift to the movements of his colleagues, the sounds from the hallway, or the reflections in his monitor, his eyes darting around the room.

His commute, once a time for listening to podcasts or thinking through design problems, became an exercise in hyper-awareness. He’d walk with his head slightly swiveled, his senses finely tuned to every shadow, every person who walked past him, every vehicle that slowed nearby. The once-vibrant city now felt like a labyrinth of potential threats, demanding his unwavering attention. The relentless strain of this vigilance, combined with the crushing weight of self-blame, left him perpetually exhausted, unable to fully engage with his creative work or connect authentically with others. He found himself increasingly isolated, trapped in a cycle of internal scrutiny and external scanning. The constant mental exertion was debilitating, yet he felt powerless to stop, convinced that his safety depended on it.

It was this profound exhaustion and the realization that his life had been reduced to a perpetual state of alert that finally prompted Kwame to seek help. He yearned for a return to a time when he could trust his environment and himself, but a part of him deeply feared that such a state of peace was now an unattainable luxury, permanently out of reach in a world he perceived as inherently perilous.
